title: Core laboratory network: critical value notification timeliness measured from two years of call logs
notes: Routine path with clean inputs: a clinical biochemist plans a retrospective review of laboratory information system call logs to measure critical value notification against a 30-minute standard (routing explicit retrospective from 'retrospective review'). Two recorded fixture searches, a broad one and a targeted one on how to define the interval and on night staffing, return five and two well-formed records (2018 to 2024), each with its own retrieval event; the appraisal annotates all seven and records five source-derived claims with passages that are exact substrings of the abstracts; certainty 'moderate' over inspected records. inputs.need:
I am the clinical biochemist who leads the core laboratory for a network of three hospitals and 40 community clinics. Our policy says critical values (for example potassium above 6.2 or below 2.8 mmol/L, sodium below 120 mmol/L, glucose below 2.5 mmol/L, haemoglobin below 60 g/L, INR above 6 and positive blood cultures) must be telephoned to a responsible clinician with read-back within 30 minutes of the result being verified. The laboratory information system logs every call attempt with a time stamp, the person reached, and whether read-back was documented, but nobody has looked at these logs in a structured way. Staff tell me that results for outpatients and community clinics after 17:00 take much longer, that we sometimes cannot find anyone to call, and that at night a single technologist does the calling alongside the bench work.

I want to do a retrospective review of the laboratory information system call logs for 2024 and 2025 to measure how long notification takes from verification to successful read-back, what proportion meet the 30-minute standard, and where the delays are: by patient location (inpatient, emergency, outpatient, community clinic), time of day, analyte and number of call attempts. I would then like to know which factors are associated with delays of more than 30 minutes, so the laboratory director can decide whether to set up an escalation route for community results after hours.

The research ethics board approved the project with a waiver of consent in August, and the laboratory information system manager has agreed to provide a de-identified extract. I need help with definitions, the analysis plan and a sensible way to handle results where no successful call was ever documented.
inputs.constraints: No new data collection; the extract covers January 2024 to December 2025; about 60 hours of the laboratory quality officer's time for analysis; results needed by the laboratory director in February 2027.
localFacts: The research ethics board approved the review with a waiver of consent on 2026-08-27 (REB file 26-311).
The laboratory information system manager agreed on 2026-09-02 to provide a de-identified call-log extract for 2024 and 2025 (data request LIS-DR-2026-19).
About 14,000 critical value calls were logged across the network in 2025.
Policy LAB-POL-012 requires telephone notification of critical values with read-back within 30 minutes of verification.

records.title: Time from verification to notification of critical laboratory values: an eleven-laboratory analysis of 96,400 call-log entries
records.authors: Petrosyan-Hale D, Obi-Lindstrom K, Varga-Ashby M
records.abstract: We analysed laboratory information system call logs for 96,400 critical values from eleven hospital laboratories over one year. Median time from verification to documented read-back was 7 minutes for inpatients and 24 minutes for outpatients. Notification within 30 minutes was achieved for 94 percent of inpatient results and 71 percent of outpatient results. Outpatient results verified after 17:00 had the longest delays, and 3 percent of outpatient critical values had no successful notification documented. Results requiring three or more call attempts accounted for most delays beyond one hour. Laboratories with a written escalation route for unreachable clinicians had shorter outpatient times.

records.title: Unsuccessful call attempts and read-back documentation in critical value reporting at a regional laboratory
records.abstract: We reviewed 8,200 critical value notifications from one regional laboratory. Eighteen percent of results needed more than two call attempts before a responsible clinician was reached, most often for outpatient and community results. Read-back was not documented for 9 percent of successful calls, more often at night. Call attempts were logged reliably, but the reason a call failed was recorded as free text in fewer than half of cases. The authors recommend structured fields for failed calls and a defined escalation after the second unsuccessful attempt.

records.title: Timeliness, read-back and escalation in critical value notification: a systematic review of 31 laboratory studies
records.authors: Halvorsen-Oduya B, Castell-Mbeki R, Tan-Whitaker J
records.abstract: We included 31 studies of critical value notification from hospital and reference laboratories. Delays were consistently longer for outpatient and community results and outside working hours. Written escalation pathways were associated with shorter notification times in eight of nine studies that examined them. Studies defined timeliness differently: some measured from specimen collection, some from verification and some from the first call attempt, which made comparison difficult. Read-back documentation ranged from 78 to 99 percent. Only two studies linked notification delay to patient outcomes, both with small numbers of adverse events.

records.title: Automated secure messaging versus telephone for critical value notification: a before-after comparison
records.abstract: One hospital laboratory replaced telephone calls for selected critical values with secure messages requiring acknowledgement in the electronic record. Median time from verification to acknowledgement fell from 14 to 6 minutes. However, 12 percent of messages were not acknowledged within 30 minutes and had to be followed by a telephone call, and acknowledgement did not always mean that the clinician had read the result. The change applied only to inpatients and was accompanied by staff training. The authors caution that messaging needs a fallback call and should not be introduced for community results without an escalation route.

records.title: Community clinic critical values after hours: who is responsible when the clinic is closed?
records.abstract: This report describes how six laboratories handled critical values for community clinic patients verified after the clinic had closed. Laboratories could not reach a responsible clinician for 23 percent of such results on the first evening, mainly because on-call lists were out of date or not held by the laboratory. Staff then called the patient directly, contacted an emergency department or waited until the next morning, with no consistent rule. The committee recommends that every community clinic name an after-hours contact and that laboratories hold a current list, with a defined route when nobody can be reached.

records.title: Defining the start and end of critical value notification intervals: time-stamp validity in laboratory information systems
records.abstract: We compared laboratory information system time stamps with independent observation for 1,150 critical value notifications. Verification time stamps were accurate to within one minute in 99 percent of cases. The time of successful read-back was missing in 6 percent of logged calls, usually when the technologist completed the call record later. Collection times were unreliable for community specimens. We recommend measuring notification from verification to documented read-back, treating a missing read-back time as an unsuccessful notification in the primary analysis, and reporting how often end times are missing.

records.title: Night-shift workload and delays in critical value notification in a hospital laboratory network
records.abstract: Using two years of call logs from a three-hospital network, we examined whether notification delays were linked to night-shift staffing. When a single technologist covered both bench work and notification, the odds of a delay beyond 30 minutes were 2.1 times higher than when a second staff member was available (95 percent CI 1.7 to 2.6), after adjustment for patient location and analyte. Delays clustered in the first hour after large analyser runs. The authors suggest separating notification from bench work at night or routing night calls through a central clinical desk.

response.synthesis: Seven records retrieved in two recorded searches, appraised at abstract level. Call-log studies consistently show slower notification for outpatient and community results, especially after hours (71 against 94 percent within 30 minutes in one multicentre analysis), with repeated call attempts and unreachable clinicians as the main mechanisms. A single night technologist covering bench work is associated with more delay. Verification time stamps are reliable and read-back times are occasionally missing, which supports a verification-to-read-back interval with missing end times treated as unsuccessful. Escalation pathways are associated with shorter times, but links to patient outcomes are sparse.
response.gradeRationale: Several large call-log analyses and a review agree on where delays occur, with reliable time-stamp data; the evidence is observational but the question is descriptive. Moderate certainty about the pattern of delays; low certainty about effects of escalation routes.
response.summary: Seven records from two recorded searches appraised; five source-derived claims recorded; overall certainty moderate.

steps.note: Appraisal of the seven records from both recorded searches on the production scan path (S13); certainty moderate over inspected records (G1).

response.designSummary: Retrospective review of call logs; proportions with 95 percent confidence intervals and a multivariable model for delay beyond 30 minutes.
response.sampleSize: All critical values in two years are included, about 28,000. Precision rather than power sets the plan: a subgroup of 2,000 community results verified after 17:00 with about 70 percent notified within 30 minutes gives a 95 percent confidence interval of about plus or minus 2 percentage points. With several thousand delayed results the regression is not limited by events; parsimony comes from fixing six factors in advance.
response.primaryAnalysis: Proportion notified within 30 minutes overall and by location and time block, with 95 percent confidence intervals; mixed-effects logistic regression for delay beyond 30 minutes with location, time block, weekday or weekend, analyte group, night staffing and month as fixed effects and ordering clinic or ward as a random intercept.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Never-notified results by location and time block; median and 90th percentile time to read-back; delays by number of call attempts, reported descriptively because attempts lie on the path between location and delay.
response.missingData: A missing read-back time counts as not within 30 minutes in the primary analysis; a sensitivity analysis excludes such calls; the share of missing times is reported by subgroup.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; subgroup estimates are reported with confidence intervals and without significance claims.

Night staffing was linked from rosters. A mixed-effects logistic model with six pre-specified factors examined delay beyond 30 minutes.

I am the clinical biochemist who leads the core laboratory for a network of three hospitals and 40 community clinics. Our policy says critical values (for example potassium above 6.2 or below 2.8 mmol/L, sodium below 120 mmol/L, glucose below 2.5 mmol/L, haemoglobin below 60 g/L, INR above 6 and positive blood cultures) must be telephoned to a responsible clinician with read-back within 30 minutes of the result being verified. The laboratory information system logs every call attempt with a time stamp, the person reached, and whether read-back was documented, but nobody has looked at these logs in a structured way. Staff tell me that results for outpatients and community clinics after 17:00 take much longer, that we sometimes cannot find anyone to call, and that at night a single technologist does the calling alongside the bench work.

I want to do a retrospective review of the laboratory information system call logs for 2024 and 2025 to measure how long notification takes from verification to successful read-back, what proportion meet the 30-minute standard, and where the delays are: by patient location (inpatient, emergency, outpatient, community clinic), time of day, analyte and number of call attempts. I would then like to know which factors are associated with delays of more than 30 minutes, so the laboratory director can decide whether to set up an escalation route for community results after hours.

The research ethics board approved the project with a waiver of consent in August, and the laboratory information system manager has agreed to provide a de-identified extract. I need help with definitions, the analysis plan and a sensible way to handle results where no successful call was ever documented.
